event: Mehmed Ali's Egypt seizes Syria and Palestine: conscription, disarmament of the notables, centralized taxation — and an open door to European consulates and Christian missions. The occupation makes the Eastern Question acute: the duress under which every subsequent Ottoman concession is extracted.
src: Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997); Ma'oz, Ottoman Reform in Syria and Palestine (1968)
note: The pasha-cascade thread's opening move: it is Egyptian pressure, not Ottoman conviction, that forces Gülhane in 1839 — reform as the price of European rescue.

event: The enforcement layer arrives: the Sultan's firman (June 1838) admits a British Vice-Consulate at Jerusalem — the first Western consulate in the city; the Balta Liman commercial convention (16 Aug 1838) opens the Ottoman economy. Within months the new consul's standing instruction includes the Jews by name.
quote: that it will be a part of your duty as British Vice-Consul at Jerusalem to afford Protection to the Jews generally. (Bidwell directive, 31 January 1839)
instrument: Firman of June 1838; Balta Liman convention; FO instruction of 31 Jan 1839
src: Eliav, Britain and the Holy Land 1838–1914 (1997), pp. ~22–23, reproducing FO 78 documents
note: Pure capitulation-weakness: the Porte resisted the firman and yielded. The consular system supplies what Ottoman courts would not — enforcement — and every legal instrument in this ledger is parchment without it.

event: The Hatt-i Şerif of Gülhane opens the Tanzimat under Egyptian-crisis duress: security of life, honour and property, regular taxation — and, per Ma'oz, "for the first time in Ottoman history, officially promised equality before the law for Muslims and non-Muslims alike."
quote: only a little more than half a year after the reading and proclamation of the Hatti Sheriff of Gülhane in this country there has been a general reaction in favour of the Koran and of the exclusive privileges of the Mahometans… (Consul-General Rose, 1841)
src: Ma'oz, Ottoman Reform in Syria and Palestine 1840–1861 (1968), pp. ~21–24
note: Proclaimed and resisted at once: Rose's 1841 dispatch documents the backlash within months. The reforms were extracted, not believed — which is why they needed the consular layer to be real.

event: The restored sovereign re-charters Jewish protection: Abdülmecid's firman of 6 November 1840, secured by Montefiore's mission after the Damascus Affair, declares the ritual-murder charges "pure calumny" and pledges protection — Montefiore calls it "the Magna Carta for the Jews in the Turkish dominions."
quote: the charges made against them… are pure calumny… The Jewish nation shall possess the same privileges as are granted to the numerous other nations who submit to our authority. The Jewish nation shall be protected and defended.
src: Frankel, The Damascus Affair (1997), pp. ~377–78, quoting Montefiore, Diaries
note: Issued weeks after European arms restored Syria to the Porte — protection and dependence in a single document. The affair itself sits in the foreclosed-alternatives baseline lane.

event: The protégé system widens: with Palmerston's sanction, British protection is extended to former Russian Jews in Palestine whom Russia declined to protect — stateless Jews acquire a consular shield in Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed, and Tiberias.
instrument: FO authorization of protection for former Russian subjects
src: Eliav, Britain and the Holy Land (1997), documents on Russian-Jewish protection (Young–Palmerston correspondence)

event: The enforcement layer working, case by case: Consul Finn's records show the local order producing the abuse and the consulate providing the remedy — for Hebron Jews under oppression, robbed pedlars, a Jew beaten by a soldier.
quote: They were no longer outwardly persecuted — being well known to be under British protection.
src: Finn, Stirring Times (1878), p. 56
note: Same row anchors the foreclosed-alternatives baseline lane: security via a withdrawable external guarantor, not via the host order itself.

event: The before-marker: Montefiore's Jaffa orchard (1855) and the Mishkenot Sha'ananim land outside Jerusalem's walls each require a personal imperial firman — a sultan's individual dispensation per transaction. Two decades later, purchase is routine registration. That gap is the whole unsealing in miniature.
instrument: Personal firmans of Abdülmecid to Montefiore
src: Montefiore record (context row); cf. Schölch, Palestine in Transformation (1993) for the post-reform routine market

event: The Islahat Hatt-ı Hümayun — issued days before the Paris peace congress, under Allied pressure — decrees civil equality for non-Muslims: emancipated persons who can hold property and litigate. The status leg of the triad.
src: Ma'oz, Ottoman Reform (1968); Davison, Reform in the Ottoman Empire 1856–1876 (1963)
note: Status alone is inert: emancipated paupers, without tenure to hold or capital allowed in. And per Lewis (foreclosure-ledger baseline), the equality decree itself was experienced by much of the majority as a violation of the dhimma's established principles — the resentment that surfaces at Damascus in 1860.

event: The Land Code: registered, alienable individual title — something to buy. And a perverse second effect: fellahin under-register to dodge taxes and conscription while notables register en bloc, so the code manufactures concentrated absentee title — the seller class whose consolidated tracts later make purchase-at-scale possible.
quote: the Arab rural cultivators, unless they are transferring land to townsmen or to some non-Arab who insists on registration, keep clear of the Land Registry. (Mandate director of land settlement, quoted in Stein)
src: İnalcık & Quataert, ESHOE (1994); Stein, The Land Question in Palestine (1984), pp. ~12–13, 65; Schölch (1993)
note: Stein documents the mechanism into the Mandate: peasants mortgaging land for military-exemption fees, registration in fictitious names, absentee books. Without the concentration, acquiring a valley means ten thousand fellah-by-fellah transactions — impossible.

event: After the Damascus massacre and the Lebanon war: a French expeditionary force lands, and the 1861 Règlement Organique makes Mount Lebanon an autonomous mutasarrifate under a European-guaranteed Christian governor. The external-guarantor pattern is formalized at province scale.
src: Mishaqa (Thackston tr. 1988) — massacre primary; Ma'oz (1968)
note: The precedent the Porte read forward: European-patronized minority + weak center = carved-off province. Greece, Serbia, Bulgaria and the Armenian question complete the template that makes Jewish concentration in Palestine look, to Yıldız, like the same play.

event: The foreign-ownership law (with its 1868 protocol): foreign nationals may acquire real estate in the empire, their tenure backed by the capitulations. The diaspora's capital is admitted to the market — the third leg of the triad.
instrument: Law on foreign ownership of real property, 1867 (Safer law)
src: Stein, The Land Question (1984); Mandel (1976) — 'their right under the 1867 Land Code to acquire land'
note: The stack is now complete and each leg needs the others: status without tenure makes emancipated paupers; tenure without foreign access keeps Rothschild's money in Paris; and all three are parchment without the consular enforcement layer of 1838.

event: The state manufactures the seller class: the government sells the land of 17 villages in the Marj ibn ʿAmir (1869), then five more (1872), to Beirut businessmen — the Sursuqs taking the lion's share: some 230,000 dunums for £20,000. Thirty villages of tenants under one absentee firm.
quote: The whole plain of Esdraelon… is now all owned by one rich firm of Syrian bankers… They own practically about five thousand human beings as well, who form the population of thirty villages. (Oliphant, 1883)
src: Schölch, Palestine in Transformation (1993), pp. ~114–15
note: Precision against the shorthand: Schölch documents two government sales (1869, 1872), not a single auction; Nazareth notables' protest even clawed back part of the 1869 sale. It is these consolidated tracts that the Zionist institutions buy from the Sursuq heirs in the 1920s (Stein) — the land-regime page carries that half.

event: The substrate fails fiscally: the debt moratorium of 1875–76, then the Decree of Muharrem (1881) creates the European-run Public Debt Administration — the state's own revenues pass under foreign administration in the same year it begins attempting demographic sovereignty over one district.
quote: In the Ottoman Empire, this crisis led, in 1881, to the Public Debt Administration. The formation of this organization… guaranteed that the state would honor its obligations and had accepted its status as a debtor nation in the world financial system.
src: İnalcık & Quataert, An Economic and Social History of the Ottoman Empire (1994), pp. ~774–75
note: The 1869/1872 land sales above are the same weakness in another register: a cash-starved state selling villages. A warden this poor can decree a cap; it cannot staff one.

event: The cap: Jewish immigrants may settle anywhere in the empire except Palestine — concentration is the fear, not Jews. Having watched Greece, Serbia, Bulgaria and the Armenian question run the European-patronized-minority template, the Porte reads Zionism as the same play, and rations the one district.
src: Mandel, The Arabs and Zionism Before World War I (1976), ch. 1
note: Band-width tracked imperial confidence: the strong sixteenth-century empire absorbed the entire Sephardi expulsion and let Salonika become a Jewish-plurality city; the weak nineteenth-century one rations a few thousand entries at Jaffa. Companion row on the foreclosed-alternatives ledger carries the asymmetry with contemporaneous Muslim in-migration.

event: The land leg is capped too: the Mutasarrif of Jerusalem is ordered to stop sales of miri land to Jews "even if they were Ottoman subjects." The embassies protest a "manifest breach" of the Capitulations — and by 1893 extract a concession. The seal leaks the year it is set.
quote: In November 1892 the Mutasarrif of Jerusalem was ordered to stop the sale of miri land… to Jews, even if they were Ottoman subjects… The embassies in Constantinople took up their cause, protesting a 'manifest breach' of the Capitulations… the Powers were able, in 1893, to extract a concession.
note: The same capitulatory layer that protects Jewish buyers is what gutted the sovereignty attempting the prohibition — the double edge in a single episode.

event: The sovereign refuses the charter at any price. Abdülhamid's answer to Herzl, relayed by Newlinski and recorded in Herzl's diary, June 1896 — charter diplomacy continues to 1902 and dies with it.
quote: I cannot sell even a foot of land, for it does not belong to me, but to my people… Let the Jews save their billions. When my Empire is partitioned, they may get Palestine for nothing. But only our corpse will be divided. I will not agree to vivisection.
instrument: Refusal of the Herzl charter proposals
src: Herzl, Complete Diaries (Patai ed.), June 1896, pp. ~378–79
note: Diary primary with a relay caveat: Herzl recording Newlinski recording the Sultan. Read against 1920: the empire was partitioned, and at San Remo the charter was granted by the power that won the territory — the prophecy kept almost to the letter.

event: The cap's enforcement apparatus at its most elaborate: all Jews entering Palestine surrender their papers for a three-month permit — the Red Slip — with monthly statistics, expulsion of overstayers, and officials threatened with punishment. In practice: baksheesh at every stage, overland entry via Egypt, consular vetoes on deportation — and Jews welcome the slip because it guarantees entry.
quote: Bribery ('baksheesh') was part of life in the Ottoman Empire, and the Jews could bribe any official, short of Rauf Paşa himself… Everything had its price: entry and release of baggage at the ports, permits to buy land and build on it.
note: The warden too frightened not to lock the door and too weak to keep it locked — the row is the mechanism of the leak, not the absence of the lock.

event: The Young Turks keep the cap and cannot enforce it either: as opposed to Zionism as Abdülhamid (barring a brief 1913–14 financial flirtation), they retain the old restrictions — while the community the restrictions were meant to cap doubles.
quote: Although the old regime's restrictions against the Jews were retained, they continued to be ineffective. By the outbreak of World War I, the Jewish community in Palestine had risen to about eighty-five thousand, and over forty colonies had been established.
instrument: CUP continuation of the Hamidian restrictions
note: On the order of 60,000 net entries against standing policy by 1914, from a ~25,000 base. The 1911 parliamentary debate (foreclosed-alternatives ledger) is this policy defending itself in public.

event: The enforcement layer dies first: on entering the war the CUP unilaterally abrogates the capitulations (announced 9 September 1914, effective 1 October). The consular shield that had protected foreign-subject Jews — and gutted every Ottoman attempt at demographic sovereignty — is gone at a stroke.
src: Context row; İnalcık & Quataert (1994) on the capitulatory regime
note: What follows immediately shows what the shield had been worth: deportations of enemy-subject Jews, and wartime coercion checked only by German and American pressure.

event: The warden's last years: famine, disease, deportations, the forced evacuation of Jaffa–Tel Aviv (April 1917), the Nili hangings — the Yishuv falls from roughly 90,000 to under 60,000, under a regime that had just demonstrated on the Armenians what it could do to a suspect minority in a strategic zone.
src: Segev, One Palestine, Complete (2000), Part I
note: Cross-listed on the foreclosed-alternatives ledger (Ottomanism lane). Jamal's harsher instincts were checked contingently by German and American pressure — external-guarantor dependence to the very end of the old order.

event: The ground changes hands: Balfour Declaration (2 Nov 1917), Allenby enters Jerusalem (Dec 1917), Mudros ends Ottoman rule (Oct 1918). The boundary track opens at a stroke — the door swings open over a community that barely survived the opening.
src: Context row; Mandate preamble (foreclosed-alternatives ledger carries the text)

event: The new sovereign's first land act is a freeze: the military administration closes every Land Registry office (18 Nov 1918) — partly to stop foreclosure on peasants who had mortgaged land to buy Ottoman military exemptions — and all transactions are forbidden until 1 October 1920.
quote: In an effort to avoid conscription, many peasants in Palestine before and during the war purchased military exemptions using their lands for collateral.
src: Stein, The Land Question (1984), pp. ~11–12
note: Also the tell on the 1858 registers: what reopened in 1920 was a record full of fictitious names, evasions, and absentee title — the raw material of the Mandate land question.

event: San Remo (Apr 1920) assigns the Mandate; the League approves it (Jul 1922); Lausanne (Jul 1923) buries the capitulations and the Ottoman claim, and the Mandate enters force (Sep 1923). The charter Herzl shopped around the concession economy for two decades is granted — by the empire that won the territory, embedded in the successor's constitutive document.
instrument: San Remo resolution; Mandate for Palestine; Treaty of Lausanne
src: Mandate for Palestine (1922); context
note: Abdülhamid, 1896: 'When my Empire is partitioned, they may get Palestine for nothing.' Every other post-Ottoman successor formalized the existing majority's primacy; this territory alone was chartered otherwise — the double-sided closure carried on the foreclosed-alternatives ledger.

event: The successor sovereign opens a regulated door: the first Immigration Ordinance fixes a quota of 16,500 Jewish immigrants for the first year. The Land Registries reopen five weeks later (1 Oct 1920). The nineteen-year legal window begins.
quote: The first Immigration Ordinance was enacted and a quota of 16,500 immigrant Jews fixed for the first year.
src: A Survey of Palestine (1946), vol. I, ch. II (26 Aug 1920)

event: First use of the lever: after the Jaffa riots, Samuel suspends Jewish immigration; it resumes under the "economic absorptive capacity" formula that the 1922 Churchill White Paper makes doctrine. Violence moves the dial — a lesson every actor records.
instrument: Immigration suspension, May 1921; Cmd. 1700 absorptive-capacity rule
src: A Survey of Palestine (1946), ch. II; Cmd. 1700 (foreclosed-alternatives ledger row)

event: The certificate machinery consolidates: category A (capitalists — £1,000 and upwards), B (dependants), C (labour schedule, negotiated half-yearly, distributed by the Jewish Agency), D (students/professionals). Entry becomes an administered, bargained pipeline — with the JA inside the machine.
quote: The following categories of immigrants were permitted… A.-(i) Persons in possession of £1,000 and upwards, and their families…
src: Hope Simpson, Cmd. 3686 (1930), ch. on immigration machinery
note: The £1,000 capitalist category is why the Fourth and Fifth Aliyot skew middle-class: the door's shape selected the migrants.

event: The zigzag: Hope Simpson and the Passfield White Paper move to restrict land transfer and immigration on Article 6 grounds; the MacDonald Letter (Feb 1931) walks it back under Zionist and parliamentary pressure. Each side learns the same lesson — the sovereign's line moves under pressure.
src: Cross-reference: foreclosed-alternatives ledger 1930–31 row (Hope Simpson PRIMARY-DIRECT)
note: Arabs read the Letter as proof London yields to Zionist pressure ('the Black Letter'); Zionists read Passfield as proof the Mandate could be reversed. The zigzag radicalizes both.

event: The effective open segment: registered Jewish immigration runs 9,553 (1932) → 30,327 (1933) → 42,359 (1934) → 61,854 (1935, the peak year of the entire Mandate). Through this slot — with 1920–26 — passes essentially the demographic basis of the state.
quote: 1935: 64,147 total — 61,854 Jews, 903 Arabs, 1,390 others. (Survey immigration table)
instrument: Labour schedules + capitalist certificates at full flow
src: A Survey of Palestine (1946), immigration tables, ch. VII
note: The legal window 1920–May 1939 is nineteen years; the practically open segments are roughly 1920–26 and 1932–36 — call it eleven effective years, with 1927 running net-negative in mid-recession. 56,000 to 475,000 through those slots.

event: Politics replaces absorptive capacity: on Peel's recommendation a "political high level" caps Jewish immigration at 12,000 a year — "in no circumstances" more — enacted in the Immigration (Amendment) Ordinance 1937, the High Commissioner acting "in his unfettered discretion." Actual 1937 entries: 10,536, down from 61,854 two years earlier.
quote: there should be a political high level of Jewish immigration to cover all categories and that the level should be fixed for the following 5 years at 12,000 a year and that in no circumstances during that period should more than that number be allowed…
src: A Survey of Palestine (1946), ch. VII, ¶25–26
note: The gates are tightening two years before the White Paper formalizes closure — the cruelest sequencing in the file: the door shuts in the season the need becomes existential.

event: The successor sovereign's Hamidian moment: 75,000 over five years, then nothing without Arab acquiescence. But the same instrument lands on a different object: the 1881 cap fell on ~25,000 subsidized dependents and yielded leakage and compliance; the 1939 cap falls on ~475,000 with a para-state, a trained officer cadre, and a fleet-improvising Mossad le-Aliyah Bet.
src: Cmd. 6019 (foreclosed-alternatives ledger row, PRIMARY-DIRECT via Barbour/Khalidi)
note: Suppression before the tracks matured caps the movement; suppression after merely selects its enemies — what the cap produced was Lehi, the blockade war, and the insurgency that helped exhaust the patron.

event: The land market re-freezes: the Land Transfers Regulations prescribe zones where transfer "save to a Palestinian Arab is prohibited," zones at the High Commissioner's discretion, and a free zone — the chartered patron re-imposing, in the majority's protection, the seal the Hamidian state had attempted in 1892. A Jewish general strike answers the next day.
quote: certain areas were prescribed in which the transfer of land save to a Palestinian Arab is prohibited except in certain stated circumstances, others in which the transfer… is subject to the discretion of the High Commissioner, and others in which there are no restrictions.
src: A Survey of Palestine (1946), ch. II (28 Feb 1940) + land chapter ¶89

event: The cap meets a navy: unlike the Ottoman seal, the British one is enforced — patrols, deportations, Patria, Struma, the Cyprus camps. And it still leaks: Aliyah Bet turns illegal entry into the movement's central political weapon, and every intercepted ship into a case against the patron.
src: Cross-reference: foreclosed-alternatives ledger blockade row; framework §2–3
note: Enforcement without legitimacy: the images of 1947 (Exodus) do to the British position what baksheesh did to the Ottoman one — dissolve it, by a different solvent.

event: The second cash-starved empire over the same ground in seventy years: a ~100,000-man garrison against an insurgency, postwar austerity and the 1947 sterling crisis at home, India going — in February 1947 Bevin refers Palestine to the United Nations. The patron is exhausted before the question is answered.
instrument: Referral of Palestine to the UN, Feb 1947
src: Context row; Segev, One Palestine, Complete (2000), closing chapters
note: Echo of 1875–81: the sovereign's fiscal collapse precedes and predicts its abdication of demographic sovereignty. The substrate fails the same way twice.

event: The second imperial death over the same ground in thirty years: withdrawal without a successor regime — no cooperation with partition implementation, no transitional authority. The ground passes to whoever can hold it.
src: Cross-reference: foreclosed-alternatives ledger withdrawal row (Morris; UNSCOP A/364)
note: Removal test, run on the whole file: no Ottoman collapse → the cap holds, the Yishuv plateaus as a capped millet, no charter exists — and after 1924, no American exit either. The substrate had to fail in a particular way: slowly enough to leak for forty years, then suddenly enough to be replaced by a charter-bound patron rather than a consolidated successor.
